findings.title: KeyError when Integration has no 'sender' in metadata during install check
findings.body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally on the path where an Integration row exists but no OrganizationIntegration does. The `sender` key is only written when the integration was created from the installation webhook (or when `state.get("sender")` was set, which nothing in this pipeline does). Integrations created through the pipeline itself (e.g. when the installation webhook was delayed, lost, or raced with the pipeline finish), or legacy Integration rows created before sender tracking, have no `sender` in metadata. When such an installation is later added to another organization (Integration exists, OrganizationIntegration deleted after uninstall, Integration still ACTIVE), this line raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the intended error/success page. Additionally, `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` returns None for pipelines created before this step existed, silently failing the comparison. Use `.get()` chains with sensible defaults for both lookups.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the 404/'installation could not be found' branch
findings.body: The test previously verified that a 404 from GitHub's `/app/installations/{id}` endpoint surfaces the message "The GitHub installation could not be found." (raised by GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration). After this change, the test sends a deliberately wrong `state` value ('ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05') and only asserts the state-mismatch message "Invalid installation request."; the 404 stub added via `responses.replace` is never exercised because the pipeline errors out at the OAuth step before build_integration runs. The `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` branch now has zero test coverage, and the test name no longer describes what it tests. Add a test that completes the OAuth step with a valid state and a 404 installation lookup.

findings.title: No positive test for the sender-match path (OAuth user == installer)
findings.body: test_github_user_mismatch only covers the failure case (webhook sender 'attacker' vs OAuth user 'octocat'). There is no test where the webhook-created Integration's `metadata["sender"]["login"]` matches the OAuth-authenticated user and the install proceeds successfully through the new check in GitHubInstallation.dispatch. Since no existing test drives the flow through an existing webhook-created Integration with a matching sender, a regression that inverts or breaks the comparison (e.g. always erroring, or a KeyError-style crash being masked) would not be caught by the suite.

findings.title: OAuth `code` is not bound to the pipeline, allowing replay against a different pipeline
findings.body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, the `state` is validated against `pipeline.signature` and the `code` is exchanged for a token, but nothing verifies that the `code` was issued for *this* pipeline's authorize request. The tests show `pipeline.signature` is deterministic and identical across different organizations and users (the same value '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' works for org 1, org 2, and different users), so `state` is not an instance-specific secret. Because the token exchange uses the global GitHub app client credentials, an attacker who intercepts a victim's authorization `code` (e.g. via Referer leakage or logs from the callback URL `.../extensions/github/setup/?code=...&state=...`) can replay it on their own valid pipeline before the victim does: the state check passes (it is their own pipeline), the token exchange succeeds (single-use code, first exchange wins), and `github_authenticated_user` is then bound to the *victim's* GitHub login — satisfying the new sender-match check and allowing the attacker's Sentry organization to link an installation installed by the victim. Consider binding a per-pipeline nonce into the authorize request/state and validating it, and/or verifying that the code was issued with the same state value on exchange.
